blocks.text: Two patients are told they have the same cancer, a carcinoma of the colon. One has a poorly differentiated tumour confined to the bowel wall and is cured by surgery; the other has a well-differentiated tumour that has spread to the liver and is not. Knowing the tumour type is not enough: the doctor must also say how abnormal the cells look and how far the disease has spread.

blocks.markdown: Two complementary systems describe a cancer after diagnosis. **Grading** assesses the *microscopic appearance* of the tumour cells, and estimates aggressiveness. **Staging** assesses the *extent of spread* in the patient. Both guide treatment and prognosis, but they measure different things.

blocks.title: Grade and stage
blocks.text: Grade is the degree of differentiation and proliferative activity of tumour cells on microscopy (for example well, moderately or poorly differentiated, or grade 1 to 3). Stage is the anatomical extent of the tumour: its size or depth of invasion, lymph node involvement and distant metastasis.

rows: Cell appearance: differentiation, nuclear atypia, mitotic rate
Extent of disease: local, regional and distant
Clinical examination, imaging, surgery and pathology
Generally the strongest predictor of outcome
blocks.caption: Grading versus staging.

blocks.markdown:
### The TNM system

The **TNM** system, maintained by international cancer bodies, stages most solid tumours by three components:

- **T** (primary tumour): size or depth of local invasion. **Tis** is carcinoma in situ; T1 to T4 indicate increasing size or invasion of adjacent structures; **T0** no evidence of primary tumour; **TX** cannot be assessed.
- **N** (regional lymph nodes): **N0** no regional node metastasis; N1 to N3 increasing number or extent of involved nodes (definitions vary by organ).
- **M** (distant metastasis): **M0** no distant metastasis; **M1** distant metastasis present.

The prefix **c** denotes clinical stage and **p** pathological stage (after examination of the resected specimen). Combinations of T, N and M are grouped into **stage I to IV**, where stage IV generally indicates distant metastasis. The detailed criteria of each T and N category differ between organs, so the exact definitions must be looked up for the cancer in question.

rows: Confined to epithelium; basement membrane intact
T3 is more extensive than T1
M1 means for example liver metastasis
blocks.caption: General meaning of TNM categories.

blocks.title: Reading a TNM report
blocks.prompt: A pathology report reads pT2 N1 M0 for a colon carcinoma. Interpret it.

steps.text: The prefix p means the stage is pathological, from the resected specimen.
T2: the primary tumour has invaded beyond the mucosa to a moderate depth but not through the full thickness of the wall (organ-specific definition).
N1: there is metastasis in regional lymph nodes.
M0: no distant metastasis is detected.
Node-positive disease without distant spread is stage III in the usual grouping, and has a worse prognosis than node-negative disease.

blocks.answer: A pathologically staged tumour of moderate local extent with regional node metastasis and no distant spread.

blocks.markdown:
### Why stage generally outweighs grade

Stage measures what the tumour has actually done: whether it has reached lymphatics and distant organs. Once a cancer has metastasised, local treatments such as surgery cannot remove all disease, so survival falls regardless of how the cells look. Grade is an indirect estimate of behaviour and is subject to sampling error and inter-observer variation. A low-grade tumour that has spread widely has a worse outlook than a high-grade tumour found early and removed completely. Stage therefore is generally the stronger predictor of survival, although grade provides independent additional information, and in some cancers (for example soft tissue sarcomas and prostate cancer) grade has major prognostic weight.

blocks.title: Compare two patients
blocks.prompt: Patient A: poorly differentiated colon carcinoma, T1 N0 M0. Patient B: well-differentiated colon carcinoma, T3 N2 M1. Which has the better prognosis in general, and why?

steps.text: Patient A has a high-grade tumour but it is small, node-negative and has no distant spread: stage I.
Patient B has a low-grade tumour but it has spread to distant organs (M1): stage IV.
Because stage reflects the actual spread and curability, patient A generally has the better prognosis despite the worse grade.

items: Grade comes from microscopy of the tumour; stage combines clinical, imaging and pathological information.
Stage IV usually denotes distant metastasis (M1).
Systems are organ-specific: always use the rules of the relevant cancer.
Grading criteria differ between cancers (for example Gleason in prostate, Nottingham in breast).

blocks.title: Remember the pairing
blocks.text: Grade = look of the cells under the microscope. Stage = how far it has spread in the body. Ask: 'Is this about appearance or extent?'

points: Grade describes tumour cell differentiation and proliferation on microscopy; stage describes anatomical extent of disease.
TNM records primary tumour extent (T), regional lymph node involvement (N) and distant metastasis (M).
Stage is usually the stronger prognostic factor because it reflects spread and the feasibility of complete removal.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes grade from stage?

options.text: Grade reflects differentiation of tumour cells; stage reflects anatomical extent of spread
Grade reflects extent of spread; stage reflects cell differentiation
Both measure the number of lymph nodes involved
Both are determined only at autopsy

questions.correctOptionText: Grade reflects differentiation of tumour cells; stage reflects anatomical extent of spread

distractorRationale.c: Nodal number is part of stage only.

questions.explanation: Grade is a microscopic assessment of cell appearance, and stage is an anatomical assessment of spread. They provide different information.

questions.stem: In the TNM system, what does M1 signify?

options.text: Distant metastasis is present
No distant metastasis
Regional node metastasis
Carcinoma in situ

questions.explanation: M describes distant metastasis: M0 absent, M1 present. Nodal involvement is N and the primary tumour is T.

questions.stem: A pathology report for a breast carcinoma states pT1 N0 M0. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Small primary tumour, no regional node involvement, no distant metastasis
Large primary tumour with liver metastases
Carcinoma in situ with nodal metastasis
Tumour of unknown primary

questions.correctOptionText: Small primary tumour, no regional node involvement, no distant metastasis

distractorRationale.c: In situ is Tis and N0 here.
distractorRationale.d: That would be TX or T0.

questions.explanation: T1 indicates a small or early primary tumour, N0 no regional nodes and M0 no distant spread. The prefix p indicates pathological staging.

questions.stem: A patient has a well-differentiated carcinoma that has metastasised to the liver (M1), and a second has a poorly differentiated carcinoma confined to the organ of origin. Which statement best explains why the first generally has the worse prognosis?

options.text: Stage reflects the spread and curability of the disease and is generally the stronger predictor
Well-differentiated cells are always more aggressive
Grade is determined by imaging
Metastasis does not affect outcome

questions.correctOptionText: Stage reflects the spread and curability of the disease and is generally the stronger predictor
questions.explanation: Distant metastasis makes complete surgical removal impossible, so stage usually dominates prognosis. Grade adds information but is a less direct indicator.

questions.stem: True or false: Tumour grade is based on microscopic features such as differentiation, nuclear atypia and mitotic activity.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Grade is determined by the pathologist from the appearance of tumour cells. Stage is based on extent of spread.

questions.stem: Which statement about the use of TNM is correct?

options.text: The criteria for T and N categories are organ-specific and must be applied for the cancer in question
T3 means three lymph nodes are involved
N0 means distant metastasis
M0 means the tumour is in situ

questions.correctOptionText: The criteria for T and N categories are organ-specific and must be applied for the cancer in question

distractorRationale.b: T refers to the primary tumour, not nodes.
distractorRationale.c: N0 means no regional nodal metastasis.

questions.explanation: T, N and M definitions vary between organ sites. The general principles are common, but exact thresholds must be looked up.

questions.stem: A surgeon removes a colonic carcinoma and 18 regional lymph nodes are examined. Four contain metastatic tumour. Calculate the percentage of examined nodes that are positive, to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: 4/18 = 0.222, so about 22% of nodes are positive. The presence of any regional nodal metastasis makes the tumour N-positive, and the proportion of involved nodes carries prognostic information.

questions.stem: In a published cohort, 5-year survival is 90% for patients with stage I disease and 15% for stage IV disease. Calculate the absolute difference in 5-year survival, in percentage points. (Figures are illustrative.)
questions.explanation: The difference is 90 - 15 = 75 percentage points, illustrating the large effect of stage on survival. Real figures vary by cancer type and era.

questions.stem: Differentiate tumour grade from tumour stage, giving how each is determined and an example of how each is reported.
markingGuide: Grade: microscopic differentiation, atypia and mitoses
Stage: anatomical extent: primary tumour, nodes, metastasis
Grade determined by pathologist from biopsy or resection; stage by imaging, examination and pathology
Examples: well/moderately/poorly differentiated or grade 1-3; TNM or stage I-IV
questions.explanation: Grade describes tumour cell biology, whereas stage describes tumour spread. Both are needed.

questions.stem: Explain why stage is generally a stronger prognostic factor than grade, giving one example where this might not hold.
markingGuide: Stage reflects tumour burden and spread to nodes and distant sites
Spread limits curative surgery and reflects metastatic ability
Grade is indirect, subject to sampling and observer variation
Example where grade is crucial: prostate cancer (Gleason) or soft tissue sarcoma
questions.explanation: Metastatic disease usually determines outcome. Grade remains valuable in selected tumours.
